title: ETFs
concept: An exchange-traded fund, or ETF, allows an investor to buy access to a basket of investments through a single purchase.
learningObjective: Understand how an ETF can provide access to multiple investments instead of requiring the investor to buy each one separately.
primaryMisconception: ETFs and individual stocks are identical.
secondaryMisconceptions: Every ETF contains the same investments.
Buying an ETF guarantees protection from losses.
keyTakeaway: An ETF can provide access to a basket of investments through one purchase.

screens.title: One Purchase, Many Companies?
screens.content: One purchase can give you access to dozens of companies. Did you buy one stock—or something different?
screens.illustration: A single purchase ticket opens into a basket containing several fictional company logos.

screens.title: Noah’s £100 Choice
screens.content: Noah has £100. He can buy shares in one fictional company or choose a fund containing shares from several companies.
screens.illustration: A £100 card sits between one company-share card and a sealed investment basket.

screens.title: Apple or Fruit Basket?
screens.content: Buying one stock is like choosing one apple. Buying an ETF can be like choosing a basket containing several kinds of fruit.
screens.illustration: One apple appears beside a basket containing apples, bananas, oranges, and grapes.

screens.title: Following a Group
screens.content: Some ETFs follow a market index—a selected group used to measure how certain investments perform.
screens.illustration: A checklist of fictional companies connects to an ETF basket and a performance gauge.

screens.title: What Did Noah Buy?
screens.question: Which choice gives Noah access to several investments through one purchase?

options.text: One company’s stock
options.response: One stock normally provides ownership in one company, so the result depends heavily on that company.

options.text: An ETF containing several companies
options.response: Good thinking. One ETF purchase can provide access to a collection of investments.

options.text: A market index itself
options.response: An index measures a selected group. Some ETFs are designed to follow it, but the index itself is not a company share.

options.text: A guaranteed-profit account
options.response: An ETF can rise or fall in value. A basket of investments does not guarantee a profit.

screens.title: Stock, ETF, or Index?
screens.instruction: Match each investing term with its correct meaning.

educationalAssumptions: All companies and investments in this activity are fictional.
A single stock represents ownership in one company.
An ETF is a fund whose shares can be bought and sold through a market.
An ETF may contain company shares, bonds, or other investments.
Many ETFs follow a market index, but ETFs can follow different strategies.
Investors own shares of the ETF rather than directly owning each underlying investment.
Different ETFs contain different holdings and may charge different fees.
Holding several investments may spread risk but cannot prevent every loss.
The activity does not recommend buying any real ETF or stock.

rightSideItems.label: A basket of investments accessed through one purchase
A selected group used to measure investment performance

correctPairs.explanation: A stock is a small ownership share in one company. Its result depends heavily on that company’s performance and market price.
An ETF combines multiple investments inside one fund. Buying an ETF share gives access to that basket.
An index tracks the performance of a chosen group. Some ETFs are designed to follow that group.

incorrectMatchFeedback.feedback: A single stock normally represents one company. An ETF may contain a basket of different investments.
A stock is ownership in a company. An index measures the performance of a selected group.
An ETF is a fund that may hold several investments. A single stock represents one company.
An ETF may follow an index, but they are not identical. The ETF is the fund; the index is the group or measurement it follows.
An index is not ownership in one company. It measures a selected group of investments.
An index describes or measures a group. An ETF is one way an investor may gain access to a basket based on that group.

followUpQuestions.scenario: The Future Transport ETF holds shares in 30 transport-related companies.
followUpQuestions.question: What does one purchase of this ETF provide?

options.text: Access to the ETF’s basket of 30 companies
Complete ownership of all 30 companies
A guaranteed profit from every company
Direct control over the market index

followUpQuestions.explanation: The investor owns shares of the ETF. The ETF holds the underlying company shares.

followUpQuestions.question: If several companies inside the ETF lose value, what may happen?

options.text: The ETF’s value may also fall
The ETF must stay at the same price
The fund manager must repay every loss
The profitable companies guarantee a positive result

followUpQuestions.explanation: Spreading money across several holdings can reduce dependence on one company, but the whole basket can still lose value.

placementRules: Each term must match with one meaning.
Each meaning may be used once.
There is one correct match for each term.
The pairs may be completed in any order.
Both follow-up questions must be answered correctly.
config.validationMethod: Check all three pairs and both follow-up answers. Complete the interaction when every match and answer is correct.
config.retryBehavior: Keep correct pairs connected. Separate only incorrect pairs, show one short hint, and allow unlimited retries.

accessibilityAlternative.method: Present each term with three radio-button definitions. After matching, present the two follow-up questions in a linear format.
accessibilityAlternative.screenReaderInstruction: Choose the correct meaning for Single Stock, ETF, and Market Index. Then answer the two ETF scenario questions.

feedback.success: Perfect match! You separated one-company ownership, an ETF basket, and the index an ETF may follow.
feedback.incorrect: Look for the key difference: one company, one investment basket, or one group used for measurement.
feedback.incomplete: Complete all three matches and answer both ETF questions before finishing.

screens.title: One Fund, Many Possible Holdings
screens.content: You matched an ETF, or exchange-traded fund, with a basket of investments. Buying one ETF share can provide access to several companies, bonds, or other assets without buying each separately. Many ETFs follow a market index, while others use different strategies. An ETF is not identical to a single stock, and different ETFs can contain very different investments. A broader basket may spread risk, but its value can still fall and fees can reduce results.
screens.simpleSummary: One ETF purchase can provide access to several investments.
screens.illustration: One ETF share opens into several investment cards while a single-stock card remains connected to only one company.

screens.title: The Gaming ETF
screens.content: A fictional gaming ETF contains shares in console, software, chip, and online-game companies. Buying one ETF share gives access to the combined basket. If the gaming industry struggles, several holdings may fall together, so the ETF can still lose value.
screens.illustration: One ETF card opens into four gaming-industry company cards with mixed upward and downward arrows.

questions.text: Which purchase is most likely to provide access to several companies at once?

options.text: One share of an ETF holding 50 companies
options.feedback: Correct. The ETF contains a basket of 50 company holdings.

options.text: One share of a single company
options.feedback: A single stock normally represents ownership in one company.

options.text: A gift card
options.feedback: A gift card provides spending credit, not access to an investment portfolio.

options.text: One company bond only
options.feedback: That purchase provides exposure to one bond issuer rather than a basket of companies.

questions.correctExplanation: The ETF contains a basket of 50 company holdings, so one ETF purchase provides access to the combined portfolio.
questions.misconceptionTested: An ETF and a single-company investment provide identical exposure.

questions.text: Which statement correctly compares an ETF with an individual stock?

options.text: An ETF may hold many investments; a stock represents one company
options.feedback: Correct. They may both trade through markets, but they represent different structures.

options.text: They are always identical
options.feedback: Both may be traded through markets, but an ETF is a fund and a stock represents one company.

options.text: Every ETF owns the same companies
options.feedback: ETFs follow different indices or strategies and can contain very different holdings.

options.text: Both guarantee a profit
options.feedback: Stocks and ETFs can both fall in value.

questions.correctExplanation: A single stock is ownership in one company. An ETF is a fund that may contain many different holdings.
questions.misconceptionTested: ETFs and individual stocks are identical.

questions.text: An ETF holds 100 companies, but most are in the same struggling industry. What should an investor understand?

options.text: Many holdings do not remove risk when they face similar problems
options.feedback: Correct. The number of holdings matters, but their similarities also matter.

options.text: The ETF cannot lose money
options.feedback: Every ETF can lose value when its underlying holdings fall.

options.text: One hundred holdings guarantee diversification
options.feedback: A fund can hold many investments that are still exposed to the same industry or risk.

options.text: The manager must repay any fall
options.feedback: Fund managers manage the portfolio but do not guarantee or personally repay investment losses.

questions.correctExplanation: The number of holdings matters, but their similarities also matter. Companies in the same industry may fall together.
questions.misconceptionTested: Buying an ETF guarantees protection from losses.

screens.headline: ETF Basket Builder!
screens.message: You learned how one ETF purchase can provide access to several investments while still carrying risk.
screens.progressMessage: Mission 18 complete in Become an Investor.
screens.nextMissionTeaser: Next, explore how spreading money across different investments can change portfolio risk.
screens.animation: One ETF ticket opens into several company and bond cards, followed by a balanced risk reminder.

screens.title: Design Two ETF Baskets
screens.instruction: Draw two imaginary ETF baskets with four holdings each. Give them different themes to show that ETFs do not all contain the same investments.

reviewChecklist.notes: The mission focuses on ETFs as single purchases providing access to baskets of investments.
The mission distinguishes ETFs, individual stocks, market indices, ETF ownership, underlying holdings, strategies, fees, and possible losses.
The mission uses fruit baskets, gaming companies, transport companies, matching activities, and introductory investing language suitable for teens.
The mission does not recommend any real ETF, index, company, allocation, or investment decision.
The mission states that ETFs can lose value and that diversification does not guarantee a profit.
The mission includes no predictions involving real ETFs, indices, or company prices.
Choosing individual stocks, ETFs, or not investing is discussed neutrally.
The mission explains that ETFs can use different strategies, contain different assets, charge different fees, and remain exposed to losses.
The mission uses pounds, familiar fruit comparisons, gaming companies, transport businesses, and introductory market concepts for UK teens.
The learner directly distinguishes a stock, an ETF, and a market index through matching and application questions.
The quiz addresses ETFs versus individual stocks, different ETF holdings, industry concentration, and loss risk.

reviewChecklist.item: Mission can be completed in under five minutes
reviewChecklist.notes: The mission uses three short story screens, three matching pairs, two follow-up questions, and three concise quiz questions.

reviewChecklist.item: Language matches the target reading level
reviewChecklist.notes: The language is clear, practical, respectful, and appropriate for teens aged 13–17.
